=== page 2 ===
- The reagents used for macauba oil extraction included Hexane (100%, Synth, Brazil) and Anhydrous Sodium Sulfate P.A.
- (99%, Neon, Brazil), both of which were used as received without any further treatment.

=== page 3 ===
- The extraction system consisted of three 1 L round-bottom flasks connected to Soxhlet extractors and condensers.
- In each extraction unit, 125 mL of hexane was used as the solvent for approximately 17 g of macauba palm almond, resulting in a solvent-to-sample ratio of approximately 1:7.3 (m/v).
- The extraction process was conducted for approximately 5 h at about 70 °C using heating mantles.
- After extraction, the solvent was removed using a rotary evaporator (Büchi, model R-300, 100 W) at 60 °C under controlled vacuum for approximately 10 min.
- Residual moisture was removed by adding anhydrous sodium sulfate (Na2SO4, 99%).

=== page 4 ===
- The extraction yield was 15.74 ± 2.85% (w/w), with an acid value of 3.44 ± 0.02 mg KOH· g^− 1, density of 0.917 ± 0.006 g·cm^− 3 at 20 °C, and kinematic viscosity of 29.75 ± 0.76 mm^2·s^− 1 at 40 °C.

=== page 5 ===
- The FTIR spectrum (600−4000 cm^− 1) exhibits the expected intense bands for triglyceride-rich vegetable oils.
- Consistent with Melo^16 prominent absorptions at ∼2925 and ∼2851 cm^− 1 correspond to the asymmetric and symmetric C−H stretching of methylene/methyl groups (−CH 2/−CH3) in free fatty acids and triacylglycerols, reflecting saturated sp^3 hydrocarbon chains.

=== page 6 ===
- The results indicate that the sawdust gave a tar yield of 18.3 wt% in fast pyrolysis at 500 °C and 21.5 wt% at 800 °C.
